title: Equity Capital Markets (ECM)
subtitle: IPOs, rights issues, placements and listings on the Ethiopian Securities Exchange, from product choice to a full bank mandate
summary: Learn how Ethiopian banks, insurers, state enterprises and growth companies raise equity and list on the ESX Main or Growth Board, then act as lead adviser to a bank listing by introduction with an ETB 1.5 billion capital raise.
audience: Investment banking analysts and associates, ECM deal leads, corporate finance staff and CFOs of prospective issuers, and ECMA and ESX staff. Learners should first complete Ethiopian Capital Markets Law and Regulation (2.b) and Financial Modelling and Valuation (3.a) Level 1, or have equivalent knowledge.
objectives: Explain why companies raise equity and list, and choose the right ECM product for an Ethiopian issuer
Describe the IPO process, parties and documents under Ethiopian rules, and read a prospectus critically
Assess IPO readiness and design an offer structure that meets the ESX listing rules
Price and market an offer through investor education, book-building or fixed-price methods and digital distribution
Manage listings by introduction for widely held share companies, including banks and insurers
Run rights issues and follow-ons, compute the theoretical ex-rights price and size a bank's raise from its capital needs

runningCase.name: Bank A S.C. listing and capital raise
runningCase.text: Bank A S.C. is a fictional Ethiopian commercial bank founded in 2012. It has 12,400 shareholders, 5.2 million shares of ETB 1,000 par, shareholders' equity of ETB 7.8 billion, net profit of ETB 1.17 billion in 2025/26 and audited IFRS accounts. Its shares have only ever changed hands through its own register. To support its growth plan under the risk-based capital rules of SBB/95/2025, the board wants to list on the ESX Main Board by introduction and raise ETB 1.5 billion of new shares. CFO Meron Haile has appointed the fictional investment bank Wonchi Capital S.C. as lead adviser, with deal lead Yonas Bekele and associate Liya Tadesse. The course opens with the Ethio telecom 2024 share offer as a reference case, and follows Bank A from product choice through readiness, structuring, pricing, distribution and listing to the capstone mandate plan.

modules.title: Equity products and the Ethiopian listing framework
modules.summary: Why Ethiopian issuers raise equity and list, the ECM products available to them, and the ESX Main and Growth Board tests they must pass.
objectives: Weigh the benefits and costs of raising equity and listing for an Ethiopian issuer
Match an issuer's need to the right ECM product: IPO, follow-on, rights issue, private placement, employee plan or privatization offer
Test an issuer against the ESX Main Board (Rule 5.1) and Growth Board (Rule 6.1) criteria, including float and the insider moratorium
Draw lessons for deal design from the Ethio telecom 2024 share offer

lessons.title: Why raise equity and why list
body: Equity is permanent capital: it carries no fixed repayment and absorbs losses, which is why banks, insurers and fast growing companies need it. Listing adds four more things. It gives existing holders liquidity, puts a market price on the company, raises its profile with customers and lenders, and makes the next raise easier because investors already know the stock.

Listing also has costs that an adviser must put on the table early. There are one-off costs (advisers, auditors, ECMA and ESX fees, marketing), recurring costs (continuous disclosure, investor relations, a stronger board and audit function) and the discipline of public scrutiny. A founder who dislikes publishing results twice a year will find listing painful.

For Ethiopian issuers the arithmetic has changed since the ESX opened in January 2025. Banks face the risk-based capital rules of SBB/95/2025, many share companies already have thousands of holders with no way to trade, and the state has started to sell minority stakes in public enterprises. Each of these is an ECM mandate.

left.title: What listing gives
items: A market price for the shares
Profile with customers, lenders and staff

right.title: What listing costs
items: Adviser, audit, ECMA and ESX fees
Public scrutiny of results and pay

example.title: Bank A's board debate
example.text: At Bank A S.C.'s strategy retreat, director Kebede Wolde argued that 12,400 shareholders were already 'public' in all but name, trading shares through the bank's own register at prices nobody could check. CFO Meron Haile added that the bank's growth plan needs about ETB 1.5 billion of new capital within a year. The board concluded that a listing with a capital raise answered both problems, and asked for adviser proposals.

lessons.tip: Start every ECM pitch with the issuer's need (capital, liquidity, exit, compliance), not with the product.

lessons.title: The ECM product set
body: An initial public offering (IPO) offers shares to the public for the first time, usually with a listing. A follow-on is a later offer by a listed company. A rights issue offers new shares to existing holders in proportion to their holdings, which respects their pre-emption rights. A private placement sells shares to a small number of selected investors without a full public offer.

Two more products matter in Ethiopia. Employee share plans let staff buy or receive shares, often through a reserved tranche at listing. Privatization offers sell part of a state enterprise to the public, as with Ethio telecom in 2024. A listing by introduction lists existing shares without selling any, and is the natural route for widely held share companies.

Products combine. Bank A's mandate is a listing by introduction for its 5.2 million existing shares plus a primary offer of new shares, with tranches for retail, institutions, the diaspora and employees.

regulation.source: ECMA Directive No. 1030/2024, public offer and trading of securities (reported in the program register, text to confirm)
regulation.text: The directive is reported to set the registration and prospectus regime for public offers, offer periods, and a private placement exemption limited to 100 investors. Confirm the exact conditions in the official text before structuring a placement.

scenario.title: Choosing the product
scenario.situation: Abay Edible Oil S.C. is unlisted, has 85 shareholders and needs ETB 400 million within four months to build a refinery line. Two pension funds and an insurer have expressed interest, and the founders do not want public reporting yet.
scenario.question: Which product fits best?
options: A private placement to a small group of qualifying investors, with listing considered later
A full IPO on the Main Board
scenario.explain: A placement raises money quickly from known investors without a prospectus-based public offer. An introduction raises no money, an employee plan is too small, and an IPO takes longer than four months and brings the reporting the founders want to defer.

lessons.title: Main Board listing criteria
body: The ESX Main Board is for established companies. Rule 5.1 of the ESX Rulebook sets the tests: market capitalization or shareholders' equity of at least ETB 500 million on listing, a 3-year track record, profit after tax at least once in the last 3 years, and accounts under IFRS or AABE standards.

The float test ensures there is a real market. At least 15% of the shares must be in public hands, held by at least 300 holders. A large company with a market capitalization of ETB 2 billion or more needs only 10%. Shares held by directors, controlling holders and their associates do not count as public.
Analysts often pass the size and profit tests and then stumble on float, because a few holders own most of the stock. Work the float out from the share register, not from the company's own estimate.

regulation.source: ESX Rulebook (December 2024), Rule 5.1, Main Board listing criteria
regulation.text: Market capitalization or shareholders' equity of at least ETB 500 million on listing; 3-year track record; profit after tax at least once in the last 3 years; IFRS or AABE accounts; public float of 15% held by at least 300 holders, or 10% if market capitalization is ETB 2 billion or more.

worked.title: Bank A against Rule 5.1

rows.label: Profit after tax
rows.value: Profitable in each of the last 3 years: passes

rows.label: Shares held by directors and holders of 2% or more
Float required (market cap at least ETB 2 billion)

worked.note: Bank A clears every Main Board test with room to spare. Its listing problems will be practical (register quality, dematerialization, NBE approvals), not eligibility.

scenario.title: A float shortfall
scenario.situation: Gondar Cement S.C. has a market capitalization of ETB 1.4 billion. Its founding family and two directors hold 89% of the shares, and the other 11% is held by 640 holders.
scenario.question: Does it meet the Main Board float test?
options: Yes, because it has more than 300 holders
No: below ETB 2 billion market capitalization it needs 15% held by at least 300 holders, so it must sell down or issue new shares
scenario.explain: The 10% float applies only at ETB 2 billion or more. At ETB 1.4 billion the test is 15% held by 300 holders, so the family must sell, or the company must issue enough new shares to the public, to lift the float to 15%.

lessons.title: Growth Board, fixed income and the insider moratorium
body: The Growth Board is for younger companies with strong growth. Rule 6.1 asks for a 2-year track record, revenue growth of 20% a year, a market capitalization of at least ETB 50 million, and a 10% float held by at least 50 holders. There is no profit test, which suits companies that are investing ahead of earnings.

On both boards, insiders may sell at most 50% of their shares within 12 months of listing. This moratorium protects new investors from founders who list and leave. The ESX also has a Fixed Income Market, where a bond listing needs a minimum issue of ETB 10 million.

Advisers use these rules in structuring. If founders want cash at listing, the sale must fit inside the 50% limit, and the remaining shares must be locked up in the register and disclosed in the prospectus.

regulation.source: ESX Rulebook (December 2024), Rule 6.1, Growth Board listing criteria
regulation.text: 2-year track record; revenue growth of 20% a year; market capitalization of at least ETB 50 million; 10% float held by at least 50 holders; no profit test. On listing, insiders may sell at most 50% of their holdings within 12 months.

worked.title: Selam Agro Processing S.C. against Rule 6.1

rows.label: Net result 2025/26
rows.value: Loss of ETB 6 million: no profit test applies

rows.label: Planned float
rows.value: 12% to about 900 investors: passes 10% and 50 holders

rows.label: Founders' 70% stake: most they may sell in year 1

worked.note: Selam fails the Main Board profit and size tests but fits the Growth Board. The founders' sale must stay within the 50% moratorium.

example.title: Why the Growth Board suited Selam
example.text: Selam Agro Processing, a fictional Hawassa food processor, had spent two years building a cold chain and was loss-making. Its adviser, Liya Tadesse, showed the board that the Growth Board had no profit test and that 25% growth cleared the 20% bar. The founders, who had hoped to sell 60% of their stake, scaled their sale back to under half to meet the moratorium.

scenario.title: The founder's exit
scenario.situation: A founder holding 4 million shares in a company listing on the Growth Board wants to sell 2.6 million shares in the offer to fund a new venture.
scenario.question: What should the adviser say?
options: Fine, there is no limit on the Growth Board
He may sell all his shares if the float rises
He may sell at most 2 million shares (50%) within 12 months of listing, so the sale must be cut or deferred
scenario.explain: Insiders may sell at most 50% within 12 months. Selling 2.6 million of 4 million is 65%, above the limit.

lessons.title: Case: the Ethio telecom 2024 share offer
body: In late 2024 the state offered a minority stake in Ethio telecom to Ethiopian investors, the country's best known modern share offer. It was a privatization offer of existing shares, so the money went to the selling shareholder, not the company. As reported at launch, the offer was 10% of the company at a fixed price of ETB 300 per share, with a low minimum subscription so that small savers could take part.

Distribution was the innovation. Investors subscribed and paid through the company's own telebirr mobile wallet, which reached millions of users without a branch network of receiving banks. Investor education ran through media and the app. Take-up was reported to be well below the full amount in the first window, and the offer period was extended.

For ECM analysts the case is a template and a warning. Digital distribution can reach first-time investors at very low cost, but a fixed price set without institutional price discovery, limited liquidity before an exchange listing, and modest investor familiarity with shares can all depress demand. Check the latest reported figures before teaching the case.
points: Structure: secondary sale of a minority stake by the state
Distribution: telebirr wallet subscription and payment
Take-up: reported below target, offer period extended
Lessons: price discovery, liquidity path and investor education matter as much as reach

example.title: Applying the lessons to Bank A
example.text: Wonchi Capital S.C., Bank A's fictional lead adviser, used the case in its pitch. It proposed digital subscription through bank apps and wallets (the reach lesson), soft sounding of institutions before fixing the price (the price discovery lesson), and listing on the ESX Main Board on day one so buyers could sell (the liquidity lesson).

scenario.title: Reading the take-up
scenario.situation: A colleague says the Ethio telecom offer proves that Ethiopians do not want to buy shares.
scenario.question: Which response is most accurate?
options: Agree: demand for shares is absent
Agree, and advise all issuers to avoid retail investors
Disagree, because the offer was fully subscribed
Disagree: weak take-up in a first offer often reflects pricing, liquidity and familiarity factors that a better designed offer can address
scenario.explain: One offer's take-up depends on its own design. The lesson is to fix the design factors, not to abandon retail investors, and the offer was not reported as fully subscribed in its first window.

lessons.title: The Ethiopian issuer pipeline
body: Four groups of issuers drive Ethiopian ECM. Banks need capital under SBB/95/2025 and the ETB 5 billion paid-up minimum of SBB/78/2021, and most are already widely held share companies. Insurers are in a similar position. State enterprises may be partly sold by the government. Growth companies in agro-processing, manufacturing, logistics and technology need risk capital that banks will not lend.

Each group brings its own approvals. A bank or insurer needs NBE approval of significant shareholders, and a state enterprise sale needs government decisions on the stake and the buyers. A growth company may first need to convert from a PLC to a share company, since a private limited company cannot offer its shares to the public under the Commercial Code.
Good analysts keep a pipeline map: issuer, need, likely product, board and regulator approvals, and the earliest realistic listing date.

items.text: Capital rules, wide registers, NBE approvals

items.label: Insurers
items.text: Capital growth, NBE shareholder approvals

items.label: State enterprises
items.text: Minority stake sales to the public

items.label: Growth companies
items.text: Risk capital, Growth Board, PLC conversion

regulation.source: NBE Directive No. SBB/89/2024, persons with significant influence
regulation.text: NBE approval is required for influential shareholders of a bank (holding 2% or more), directors, the CEO and senior executives. Any allocation in a bank offer that takes an investor to 2% or more must be conditional on NBE approval.

lessons.tip: For a bank or insurer issuer, check NBE ownership approvals before you design the institutional tranche.

takeaways: Listing gives capital, liquidity, a price and profile, at the cost of disclosure, governance and fees
Match the product to the need: IPO, follow-on, rights issue, placement, employee plan, privatization or introduction
Main Board: ETB 500 million size, 3-year record, profit once in 3 years, IFRS or AABE accounts, 15% float with 300 holders (10% at ETB 2 billion or more)
Growth Board: 2-year record, 20% annual revenue growth, ETB 50 million size, 10% float with 50 holders, no profit test
Insiders may sell at most 50% within 12 months of listing
Ethio telecom showed the reach of digital distribution and the cost of weak price discovery and liquidity

quiz.q: Which product lists existing shares without raising new money?
quiz.explain: An introduction admits existing shares to trading; no shares are sold.

quiz.q: A company with ETB 3 billion market capitalization seeks a Main Board listing. What float does it need?
quiz.explain: At ETB 2 billion or more the float requirement falls to 10%, still with at least 300 holders.

quiz.q: Which Growth Board test does not exist on the Main Board?
quiz.explain: Only the Growth Board has a revenue growth test; it replaces the Main Board's profit test.

quiz.q: A founder holds 1 million shares at listing. How many may he sell in the first 12 months?
quiz.explain: Insiders may sell at most 50% of their holding within 12 months.

quiz.q: In the Ethio telecom 2024 offer, who received the sale proceeds?
quiz.explain: It was a sale of existing shares, so proceeds went to the seller, not the company.

quiz.q: Why might a growth company need to change its legal form before an IPO?
options: A PLC cannot offer shares to the public; it must become a share company
The Growth Board accepts only partnerships
quiz.explain: Under the Commercial Code a private limited company cannot make a public offer of shares.

modules.title: The IPO process, the prospectus and readiness
modules.summary: Run an Ethiopian IPO from readiness to listing day, read a prospectus critically, and assess whether an issuer is ready.
objectives: Sequence the IPO process from readiness to listing and name the parties and documents at each step
Compute the ECMA registration fee for a share offer under Directive No. 996/2024
Read a prospectus critically: risk factors, use of proceeds, financials, valuation and offer terms
Assess IPO readiness across governance, reporting, systems, tax and group structure, and plan the fixes

lessons.title: The IPO process step by step
body: An Ethiopian IPO moves through nine steps. The issuer assesses readiness, appoints advisers, and the advisers run due diligence. The team drafts the prospectus and files for registration with ECMA, and applies to the ESX for listing. Once approved, the offer is marketed, subscriptions are collected, shares are allocated and the shares are listed.

Each step has an owner. The lead adviser (a licensed investment bank) runs the timetable and the prospectus. Lawyers handle legal due diligence and the company's constitutional changes. Auditors report on the financial statements. Receiving banks and wallet operators collect money. The share registrar or depository records the new holders. The board takes responsibility for the prospectus.
The critical path almost always runs through the audited accounts and the legal clean-up, not the marketing. Plan backwards from the listing date.

example.title: Bank A's adviser line-up
example.text: Bank A appointed Wonchi Capital S.C. as lead adviser, a law firm for legal due diligence and the articles of association, its external auditor to report on three years of IFRS accounts, and four receiving banks plus two wallet operators for subscriptions. The deal lead, Yonas Bekele, built the timetable backwards from a target listing date seven months out.

scenario.title: Where is the critical path?
scenario.situation: Bank A's audit of its 2025/26 IFRS accounts will be signed in month 3. Marketing can be prepared in 6 weeks. The prospectus needs the audited accounts.
scenario.question: What drives the earliest filing date with ECMA?
options: The signed audited accounts that the prospectus must contain
scenario.explain: The prospectus cannot be completed without the audited financials, so filing waits for the audit. Marketing and bank agreements can run in parallel.

lessons.title: ECMA registration and fees
body: A public offer of shares must be registered with ECMA under the Capital Market Proclamation No. 1248/2021 before it opens. ECMA reviews the prospectus for completeness and fair disclosure and issues comments; the team answers them and refiles. Directive No. 1030/2024 is reported to set the registration and prospectus content rules and offer periods.

ECMA charges a registration fee under Fee Directive No. 996/2024: ETB 300,000 plus 0.1% of the value offered for a share offer. For a bond offer the fee is ETB 150,000 plus 0.05%. The fee belongs in the deal budget from day one.
Once listed, trades carry an ECMA transaction fee of 0.15% for shares, which matters for investors and for the liquidity story you tell them.

regulation.text: Registration of a share offer: ETB 300,000 plus 0.1% of the value offered. Bond offer: ETB 150,000 plus 0.05%. Transaction fees: 0.15% of value for shares and 0.005% for fixed income.

worked.title: Bank A: ECMA fees

rows.label: Example trade after listing: 10,000 shares x ETB 1,800

worked.note: Regulatory fees are small relative to the raise. Adviser fees, marketing and management time are the bigger costs.

scenario.title: Fee for an introduction
scenario.situation: Bank A's 5.2 million existing shares will be listed by introduction alongside the ETB 1.5 billion offer of new shares. The finance team asks whether the ECMA registration fee is calculated on the ETB 9.36 billion market capitalization.
scenario.question: What is the best answer?
options: Yes, the fee is 0.1% of market capitalization
The share offer fee is on the value offered, ETB 1.5 billion; check with ECMA how the introduction itself is treated
The fee is 0.15% of market capitalization
scenario.explain: The directive bases the share offer fee on the value offered. Shares listed without an offer are not 'offered', so confirm their treatment with ECMA rather than assuming. The 0.15% is a transaction fee, not a registration fee.

lessons.title: Reading a prospectus
body: A prospectus answers five questions for an investor. What are the risks? What will the money be used for? How has the business performed? What is it worth? What exactly is on offer? An analyst reads the sections in that order, not cover to cover.

Good risk factors are specific and ranked: 'NBE approval of our 2% shareholders may delay allocations' is useful, 'the economy may slow' is not. Use of proceeds should tie to the business plan with amounts and dates. The financial section should give three years of audited IFRS statements with a clear explanation of trends. The valuation and offer terms (price, size, tranches, minimums, timetable, allocation basis, refunds) must be complete and consistent.
Cross-check: the use of proceeds should match the capital plan, the risk factors should mention every issue found in due diligence, and the numbers should reconcile across sections.

items.label: Risk factors
items.text: Specific, ranked, linked to due diligence

items.label: Use of proceeds
items.text: Amounts, dates, link to the plan

items.label: Financials
items.text: Three years audited, trends explained

items.label: Valuation
items.text: Method, peers, price rationale

items.label: Offer terms
items.text: Price, size, tranches, timetable, refunds

example.title: A gap in Bank A's first draft
example.text: Associate Liya Tadesse noticed that Bank A's draft use of proceeds allocated ETB 400 million to 'digital expansion' with no breakdown, while the board's plan showed ETB 250 million for core banking upgrades and ETB 150 million for agent network growth. She also found no risk factor on the bank's foreign currency position, which due diligence had flagged. Both were fixed before filing.

scenario.title: A weak risk factor
scenario.situation: Due diligence found that 6% of Bank A's loan book is to one hotel group, and that the exposure is on a watch list. The draft prospectus says only 'the bank faces credit risk'.
scenario.question: What should the adviser require?
options: Leave it, all banks face credit risk
Put the information on the bank's website only
A specific risk factor on the concentration and its watch-list status, consistent with the financial notes
scenario.explain: A material, known risk must be disclosed specifically. A generic statement hides what due diligence found and exposes the board and adviser to liability.

lessons.title: Readiness: governance and financial reporting
body: Readiness is the gap between how the company runs today and how a listed company must run. Start with governance: a board with independent directors, working audit and risk committees, a company secretary, related-party controls and a dividend policy. For a bank, SBB/91/2024 already demands much of this, so the gap is usually smaller than for a family company.

Financial reporting is the hardest gap. The issuer needs audited IFRS or AABE accounts for the track record period, the ability to close the books on time each half year, and clean notes on segments, related parties and contingencies. Many Ethiopian companies converted to IFRS only recently and have restated comparatives, which investors and ECMA will question.
Score each area red, amber or green, list the fixes with owners and dates, and agree with the board which reds must be green before filing.

regulation.source: NBE Directive No. SBB/91/2024, bank corporate governance
regulation.text: A bank board must have at least 9 directors, one-third independent and at least 2 women, a 6-year term limit and four mandatory committees, with NBE approval of the chief risk officer. A listing bank builds its prospectus governance section on this framework.

items.label: Governance
items.text: Independent board, committees, related-party policy

items.label: Reporting
items.text: Audited IFRS accounts, fast close

items.label: Systems and controls
items.text: Reliable data, internal audit

items.label: Tax clean-up
items.text: Open assessments settled or disclosed

items.label: Group structure
items.text: Assets and businesses in the right entity

example.title: Readiness score for Abay Edible Oil
example.text: Wonchi Capital scored fictional Abay Edible Oil S.C. red on financial reporting (only one year of IFRS accounts), red on tax (two open assessments totaling ETB 38 million), amber on governance (no independent directors) and green on systems. The adviser recommended a private placement now and an IPO in two years, once three years of IFRS accounts existed.

lessons.title: Readiness: tax clean-up and group restructuring
body: Investors will not pay full value for hidden liabilities. Tax clean-up means reconciling filed returns to audited accounts, settling or provisioning open assessments, and fixing withholding and VAT compliance. A disputed assessment that cannot be settled before the IPO must be disclosed as a risk factor and, if probable, provided for.

Group restructuring puts the right assets in the listing entity. Common Ethiopian issues: land or buildings held by founders personally, sister companies that supply the issuer on non-market terms, and businesses the investors do not want (a family hotel inside a manufacturer). Each must be transferred, priced at arm's length, or carved out before the prospectus records the group.
Restructuring takes months because it needs board and shareholder approvals, valuations and, for land, administrative transfers. Start it at the readiness stage.

worked.title: Readiness gap list for Selam Agro Processing

rows.label: Governance
rows.value: Amber: appoint 2 independent directors, form audit committee (month 2)

rows.label: Financial reporting
rows.value: Green: 3 years of IFRS accounts audited

rows.label: Tax
rows.value: Red: ETB 11 million disputed VAT assessment; settle or disclose and provide (month 3)

rows.label: Group structure
rows.value: Red: cold store land held by founder; transfer to company at independent valuation (month 4)

rows.label: Systems
rows.value: Amber: inventory system not linked to the ledger (month 5)

rows.label: Earliest filing date
rows.value: Month 5, after the two red items are cleared

worked.note: The reds set the timetable. Filing before they are fixed would put them in the risk factors and depress the price.

scenario.title: The founder's land
scenario.situation: Selam's main cold store sits on land leased in the founder's own name. The founder suggests leaving it there and charging the company rent after listing.
scenario.question: What should the adviser recommend?
options: Accept, rent is a normal cost
Transfer the land right to the company at an independent valuation before listing, or at least put an arm's-length long lease in place and disclose it as a related-party arrangement
Hide the arrangement to keep the prospectus simple
Delay the IPO by five years
scenario.explain: A core asset controlled by an insider is a governance and continuity risk. Transferring it, or locking in arm's-length terms with full related-party disclosure, protects new investors.

lessons.title: Readiness for a bank issuer
body: A bank adds a layer of regulatory readiness. It must show capital adequacy under SBB/95/2025 (CET1 7%, Tier 1 9% and total capital 11% of risk-weighted assets, with full compliance due by 31 December 2026), asset quality under the provisioning rules of SBB/90/2024, and compliance with the large exposure and related-party limits of SBB/87/2024 and SBB/88/2024.

The offer itself needs NBE engagement. Any investor taking 2% or more needs NBE approval under SBB/89/2024, and changes in share ownership of banks are subject to NBE approval rules, so allocations must be conditional and the timetable must allow for it.
Investors will compare the prospectus figures with the bank's published regulatory ratios. Any gap must be explained.

regulation.source: NBE Directive No. SBB/95/2025, risk-based capital adequacy
regulation.text: Minimum CET1 of 7%, Tier 1 of 9% and total capital of 11% of risk-weighted assets; in force 10 November 2025 with quarterly reports from Q1 2026 and full compliance by 31 December 2026.

example.title: Bank A's regulatory annex
example.text: Wonchi Capital added a regulatory annex to Bank A's prospectus showing its CET1, Tier 1 and total capital ratios for the last four quarters, its NPL ratio and provisions under SBB/90/2024, and its ten largest exposures as a percentage of total capital. Meron Haile presented the annex to the NBE before filing so that no figure would surprise the supervisor.

lessons.tip: Pre-clear a bank's offer structure with the NBE informally before you file with ECMA.

takeaways: The IPO runs readiness, advisers, due diligence, prospectus, ECMA registration, ESX approval, marketing, allocation and listing
ECMA's share offer fee is ETB 300,000 plus 0.1% of the value offered; transaction fees are 0.15% for shares
Read a prospectus by risks, use of proceeds, financials, valuation and offer terms, and cross-check them
Readiness gaps in reporting, tax and group structure usually set the timetable
A bank issuer must also show compliance with SBB/95/2025 and plan for NBE approval of 2% holders

quiz.q: What is the ECMA registration fee for a share offer of ETB 800 million?
quiz.explain: ETB 300,000 plus 0.1% of ETB 800 million (ETB 800,000) equals ETB 1.1 million.

quiz.q: Which item most often sets the IPO critical path?
quiz.explain: The prospectus cannot be filed without audited accounts and a clean legal structure.

quiz.q: Which risk factor is most useful to investors?
options: Our 6% exposure to one hotel group is on a watch list and could raise provisions
quiz.explain: Specific, quantified risks tied to due diligence findings are what investors need.

quiz.q: Under SBB/95/2025, what is the minimum total capital ratio?
quiz.explain: CET1 7%, Tier 1 9% and total capital 11% of risk-weighted assets.

quiz.q: A bank allocation would take an investor to 3%. What is needed?
options: NBE approval as an influential shareholder under SBB/89/2024
quiz.explain: Holdings of 2% or more in a bank need NBE approval.

quiz.q: Which readiness issue is best solved by restructuring before the prospectus?
options: A core asset owned personally by the founder
A typo in the offer form
quiz.explain: Insider-owned core assets should be transferred or put on arm's-length terms before listing.

modules.title: Offer structuring, pricing and valuation
modules.summary: Design the offer (primary or secondary, tranches, size and float) and set the price through fixed-price or book-building methods.
objectives: Choose between primary and secondary shares and size an offer against the issuer's need and the float rules
Design tranches for retail, institutional, diaspora and employee investors, with clawback and allocation rules
Compare fixed-price and book-building methods and set a price range
Compute the IPO discount, dilution and implied multiples, and explain stabilization concepts and their limits in Ethiopia

lessons.title: Primary and secondary shares
body: Primary shares are new shares: the company receives the cash and every existing holder is diluted. Secondary shares are existing shares sold by holders: the sellers receive the cash and the company gets nothing. Many offers combine both, and investors watch the mix closely, because a large secondary component can signal that insiders want out.

In Ethiopia the purpose usually decides the mix. A bank raising capital for SBB/95/2025 needs primary shares. A state enterprise offer like Ethio telecom is secondary. A founder-owned growth company may do both, with the secondary portion capped by the 50% insider moratorium.

For an existing share company, a primary issue also engages the Commercial Code: a capital increase needs shareholder approval, and existing holders have pre-emption rights on new shares unless the general meeting waives them for a public offer.

left.title: Primary shares
items: Typical for banks and growth capital

scenario.title: Pre-emption and a public tranche
scenario.situation: Bank A wants its ETB 1.5 billion of new shares to go partly to new retail and diaspora investors, not only to its existing 12,400 holders.
scenario.question: What corporate step is needed?
options: A general meeting resolution approving the capital increase and waiving or limiting pre-emption rights for the public tranches
scenario.explain: Existing holders' pre-emption rights apply to new shares unless the shareholders waive them. Without a waiver, the shares must first be offered pro rata as a rights issue.

lessons.title: Tranches, size and float
body: Tranches split the offer by investor type so that each group gets a fair share and the book has the right mix. A typical Ethiopian structure has a retail tranche for individuals subscribing through wallets, bank apps and branches; an institutional tranche for pension funds, insurers and companies; a diaspora tranche for Ethiopians abroad; and a small employee tranche, sometimes at a discount.

Size the offer from three directions: the issuer's need, the market's capacity, and the float rules. Too small and the shares will not trade; too large and the offer fails. A clawback rule moves unsubscribed shares from a weak tranche to a strong one, so set it before launch and disclose it.
For a bank, check every institutional allocation against the 2% NBE approval threshold and any foreign ownership limits that apply under banking law before promising it.

visual.caption: Bank A's proposed ETB 1.5 billion offer by tranche (worked example)

regulation.source: NBE Directive No. SBB/89/2024, persons with significant influence
regulation.text: Holding 2% or more of a bank makes an investor an influential shareholder who needs NBE approval. In a bank offer, any allocation that would take an investor to 2% or more is made conditional on that approval and disclosed in the offer terms.

worked.title: Bank A: offer size and dilution
worked.note: The raise adds 13.8% of the enlarged share capital to the float, on top of the shares already held by about 12,300 public holders.

example.title: Setting the clawback
example.text: Wonchi Capital proposed that unsubscribed diaspora shares move first to retail and then to institutions, and that the employee tranche fall back to retail. Yonas Bekele wrote the rule into the prospectus offer terms so that no allocation decision would be made after the books closed.

lessons.title: Valuing the issuer
body: ECM valuation is relative first. For a bank, investors look at price to book value and price to earnings, adjusted for return on equity, asset quality and capital strength. With few listed Ethiopian peers, advisers use recent private share transfers on the register, regional listed banks adjusted for country risk and inflation, and a dividend discount model as a cross-check.

Inflation and the market-based exchange rate matter. Book values in birr rise with inflation and revaluations, so a P/B that looks low may simply reflect a high cost of equity. Analysts should show their cost of equity assumption, which in birr will be well above the 16% National Bank Rate set in July 2026.
The adviser produces a fair value range, then applies an IPO discount to set the offer price.

worked.title: Bank A: implied multiples at ETB 1,800

rows.label: Book value per share (7.8 billion / 5.2 million)
Book value per share after (9.3 billion / 6,033,333)

worked.note: Return on equity of 15% (1.17 / 7.8) supports a P/B a little above 1x when the cost of equity is close to that level; the range depends heavily on that assumption.

scenario.title: Using register prices
scenario.situation: Bank A's register shows 40 private transfers last year at prices from ETB 1,100 to ETB 2,600 per share, mostly between relatives.
scenario.question: How should the adviser use these prices?
options: Use the highest price as the offer price
Average them and use the result
Ignore valuation and let the ESX set the price
Treat them as weak evidence: note the range but rely on multiples, peers and investor feedback
scenario.explain: Family transfers are not arm's-length market prices. They are a reference point, not a valuation.

lessons.title: Fixed price or book-building
body: In a fixed-price offer, the issuer sets the price before the offer opens and investors subscribe at that price. It is simple to explain to first-time retail investors and suits wallet-based distribution, but the issuer guesses demand and either leaves money on the table or risks under-subscription.

In book-building, the issuer publishes a price range; institutions bid quantities at prices within it; the book shows demand at each price; and the final price is set when the book closes. It discovers the price but needs experienced institutional investors and clear rules.

A hybrid is common in new markets: institutions are sounded or book-built first, the price is fixed, and retail then subscribes at that price. Check with ECMA how the offer period rules of Directive No. 1030/2024 apply to a two-stage timetable.

left.title: Fixed price
items: Used in the Ethio telecom offer

right.title: Book-building
items: Final price set after the book closes

worked.title: Bank A institutional soft-sounding book
worked.note: At ETB 1,900 the institutional tranche would be uncovered; at ETB 1,800 it is covered 1.45 times, leaving a cushion for retail and a healthy first day.

scenario.title: Choosing the method
scenario.situation: Bank A expects about 60% of demand from first-time retail investors through wallets and bank apps, and the rest from a dozen pension funds and insurers.
scenario.question: Which pricing method fits best?
options: Hybrid: sound out institutions to set a fixed price, then open a fixed-price retail offer
Fixed price chosen by the board with no investor input
Auction on the first trading day
scenario.explain: Institutional sounding gives price discovery; a fixed retail price keeps subscription simple for first-time investors. Pure book-building is hard for retail, and a board-only price ignores the Ethio telecom lesson.

lessons.title: The IPO discount and first-day performance
body: Issuers usually price an IPO below estimated fair value. The discount rewards investors for buying an unproven stock, compensates for limited liquidity, and leaves room for a positive first day, which helps the next issuer and the issuer's own follow-on.

Too large a discount transfers value from existing holders to new ones; too small a discount risks a failed offer and a falling price. In a young market with untested liquidity, discounts tend to be larger. The adviser must explain the discount to the board in birr, not only in percent.

Stabilization is the practice of a stabilizing manager buying shares in the market after listing to support the price, often funded by over-allotting shares. It needs explicit legal permission and disclosure. Ethiopian rules on stabilization are not in the texts available to this course, so do not plan on it without ECMA confirmation.

worked.title: Bank A: IPO discount

rows.label: Value transferred to new investors (300 x 833,333)
Value per existing share (250 million / 5.2 million)

worked.note: The board is giving up about ETB 48 per existing share to secure a covered offer and a liquid start. That is the number to debate, not the percentage.

example.title: The board's question
example.text: Director Kebede Wolde asked why Bank A should sell at ETB 1,800 if fair value was ETB 2,100. Yonas Bekele showed the book coverage at each price and the ETB 48 per share cost of the discount, and noted that most existing holders would also benefit from a rising price after listing. The board approved the price.

scenario.title: Stabilization in the plan
scenario.situation: A junior analyst's draft offer plan for Bank A includes a 15% over-allotment option and a 30-day stabilization period.
scenario.question: What should the deal lead do?
options: Remove it unless ECMA confirms that over-allotment and stabilization are permitted and how they must be disclosed
Keep it, it is standard everywhere
Keep it but leave it out of the prospectus
scenario.explain: Stabilization involves trading that would otherwise look like price manipulation, so it needs a clear legal basis and disclosure. Without confirmed Ethiopian rules it should not be in the plan.

lessons.title: Allocation and oversubscription
body: When demand exceeds the shares in a tranche, the basis of allotment decides who gets what. Common methods are pro rata scaling, a minimum guaranteed allocation for small applicants with the rest scaled back, and ballots. The basis must be disclosed before the offer and applied mechanically.

Retail fairness matters in Ethiopia's first offers. Guaranteeing small applicants a minimum lot spreads ownership, supports the float test and builds trust. Large applicants are scaled back and refunded.
Refunds must be fast and accurate. Wallet and app subscriptions make this easier, but the reconciliation between applications, money received and allocations must close before listing.

worked.title: Bank A retail tranche: scaling back

rows.label: Small applicants (up to 50 shares) in full

worked.note: Guaranteeing small applicants in full and scaling the rest at 37.5% keeps ownership broad and the arithmetic transparent.

lessons.tip: Publish the basis of allotment with the results, so every applicant can check their own allocation.

takeaways: Primary shares fund the company and dilute holders; secondary shares fund the sellers
A capital increase in a share company needs shareholder approval, and pre-emption must be respected or waived
Tranches, clawback and allocation rules must be set and disclosed before launch
Fixed price suits retail; book-building discovers price; a hybrid fits Ethiopia's new market
State the IPO discount in birr per existing share, and do not plan stabilization without confirmed rules

quiz.q: A company raises ETB 600 million at ETB 400 per share and has 6 million shares before the offer. What stake do new investors hold?
quiz.explain: 600 million / 400 = 1.5 million new shares; 1.5 / 7.5 million = 20%.

quiz.q: Which offer component sends cash to existing holders?
quiz.explain: Secondary shares are sold by existing holders, who receive the proceeds.

quiz.q: Fair value is ETB 500 and the offer price is ETB 425. What is the IPO discount?
What is the main advantage of book-building?
options: It discovers the price from institutional demand
It removes the need for ECMA registration
quiz.explain: Bids at each price show the demand curve.

quiz.q: What moves unsubscribed shares from a weak tranche to a strong one?
quiz.explain: The clawback rule, set and disclosed in advance, reallocates shares between tranches.

quiz.q: Why is a bank's P/B in birr hard to compare with foreign peers?
options: Inflation, exchange rate moves and a higher birr cost of equity change what a fair multiple is
quiz.explain: Country risk, inflation and the cost of equity drive the fair multiple.

modules.title: Marketing, distribution and listings by introduction
modules.summary: Educate a new investor base, distribute through wallets, apps and receiving banks, and list a widely held share company by introduction.
objectives: Plan investor education and roadshows for a market of first-time investors
Set up digital and branch subscription channels and reconcile subscription money
Prepare a widely held share company for listing by introduction: register clean-up and dematerialization
Plan first-day price discovery for shares that have never traded on an exchange

lessons.title: Investor education in a new market
body: Most Ethiopian retail investors have never bought a listed share. Before they can judge an offer they need to know what a share is, how the ESX works, how to open an account with a broker, how prices move and how dividends are paid. Investor education is therefore part of the deal, not a public relations extra.

Education must be fair and balanced. Materials should explain risks as clearly as benefits, match the prospectus, and avoid promises of returns. Use short videos, radio in local languages, branch sessions and in-app guides, and track questions to update the FAQ.
Institutional marketing is different: analyst presentations, one-on-one meetings with pension funds and insurers, and site visits. Diaspora roadshows can run online across time zones.

items.label: Weeks 1 to 4 before launch
items.text: General education: what a share is, how ESX works, opening a broker account

items.label: Weeks 2 to 3 before launch
items.text: Institutional soft sounding and analyst briefings

items.label: Launch week
items.text: Prospectus published, retail campaign, diaspora webinars

items.label: Offer period
items.text: Branch sessions, in-app guides, FAQ updates

items.label: After listing
items.text: How to trade, read results and receive dividends

example.title: Bank A's 'Own a share' campaign
example.text: Bank A ran four weeks of education before launch: two-minute videos in Amharic, Afaan Oromo and Tigrinya, branch evenings in 40 towns, and a quiz in its mobile app. Every message was checked against the prospectus by compliance. Questions from the first week showed that many customers thought dividends were guaranteed, so the campaign added a clear message that they are not.

scenario.title: A promising slogan
scenario.situation: The marketing agency proposes the slogan 'Bank A shares: double your money with Ethiopia's growth' for the retail campaign.
scenario.question: What should the adviser say?
options: Approve if used only on radio
Approve if the board signs it
Reject: it implies a return the prospectus cannot support; use a balanced message that mentions risk
scenario.explain: Offer communications must be fair, balanced and consistent with the prospectus. A promise of doubling misleads first-time investors.

lessons.title: Digital subscription and receiving banks
body: Subscriptions can come through mobile wallets, bank apps, internet banking and branches of receiving banks. Digital channels reach far more investors at low cost, as Ethio telecom showed with telebirr, and make refunds easier. Branches remain important for older investors and larger applications.

Each channel needs the same controls: identity check (ideally through Fayda digital ID), a confirmed broker or depository account to receive the shares, the investor's acceptance of the prospectus terms, and payment into a segregated offer account that nobody can use before allocation.
Receiving banks and wallet operators sign agreements covering fees, data formats, daily reporting, cut-off times and refunds. The lead adviser reconciles every channel daily.

items.label: Identify
items.text: Fayda or other KYC, eligibility for the tranche

items.label: Account
items.text: Broker or depository account for the shares

items.label: Apply
items.text: Number of shares, accept prospectus terms

items.label: Pay
items.text: Into the segregated offer account

items.label: Confirm
items.text: Receipt with application number

worked.title: Bank A: subscription reconciliation at close

rows.label: Bank apps and internet banking: 8,300 applications
Explained: 212 branch applications paid by check, not yet cleared

worked.note: Every birr reported must be traced to the offer account before allocation. Uncleared checks stay out of the allocation until they clear or the application is rejected.

scenario.title: Using offer money early
scenario.situation: On day 5 of the offer, a receiving bank's treasury suggests placing the ETB 300 million it has collected in the interbank market overnight to earn interest for the issuer.
scenario.question: What should the lead adviser answer?
options: Agree, the interest benefits the issuer
Agree if the amount is below ETB 500 million
Let the receiving bank keep the interest
Refuse unless the offer terms and the receiving bank agreement expressly allow it; subscription money must stay segregated and available for refunds
scenario.explain: Subscription money belongs to applicants until allocation. Its handling must follow the disclosed terms; investing it without authority puts refunds at risk.

lessons.title: Listing by introduction
body: Many Ethiopian banks and insurers are share companies with thousands of holders whose shares have never traded on an exchange. A listing by introduction admits those existing shares to the ESX without an offer. The company still needs to meet the listing criteria and publish a listing document, but no money is raised.

An introduction gives existing holders liquidity and a market price, and prepares the ground for a later capital raise. It can also be combined with an offer, as in Bank A's case, so that new investors come in on day one.
The hard work is behind the scenes: the register must be clean, the shares must be held in a form the market can settle, and holders must have broker accounts so they can trade.
points: Publish a listing document approved as the rules require
Clean the share register and reconcile it to share capital
Move shares into dematerialized form with the depository
Help holders open broker accounts before day one

example.title: Bank A's register clean-up
example.text: Wonchi Capital's review of Bank A's register found 640 holders with incomplete ID records, 210 deceased holders whose shares had not been transferred to heirs, 95 holders with two entries each, and 18,400 shares where the register and the share capital account disagreed. Bank A ran a six-week campaign with branches to update records, and its lawyers handled the inheritance cases.

regulation.source: Capital Market Proclamation No. 1248/2021, Arts. 35 to 38 (exchange rules), and the ESX Rulebook (December 2024)
regulation.text: The Proclamation empowers the exchange to make listing rules, and the ESX Rulebook sets the Main Board and Growth Board criteria that apply equally to listings by introduction. An introduction raises no money but still needs a compliant listing and full disclosure.

lessons.title: Register clean-up and dematerialization
body: Dematerialization replaces paper share certificates and the company's own register with electronic records at a central securities depository, so that trades on the ESX can settle by book entry. Each holder needs an account through a broker or depository participant, and the shares are credited to it once the company's register is verified.

The order matters: clean the register, reconcile it to share capital, freeze transfers for a short period, transfer the records to the depository, and credit holders' accounts. Holders who have not opened accounts by listing day should be held in a suspense or issuer account until they do, so that their rights are protected.
ECMA's depository rules are reported but their texts were not available for this course; confirm the depository's procedures and timetable early.

worked.title: Bank A: register reconciliation before dematerialization

rows.label: Explained: 2023 bonus shares not posted to 37 holders
Explained: transfers approved but not recorded
Holders with broker accounts at listing
Shares of holders without accounts, held in suspense

worked.note: The register must reconcile exactly before shares move to the depository. A plan is also needed for the 28% of holders who are not yet ready to trade.

scenario.title: Holders without accounts
scenario.situation: Three weeks before listing, 3,500 of Bank A's 12,400 holders still have no broker account. The board asks whether to delay listing.
scenario.question: What is the best approach?
options: List on schedule, hold those holders' shares safely in a suspense or issuer account, and continue the account-opening campaign
Delay listing until every holder has an account
Cancel the shares of holders without accounts
Sell their shares on day one and send them the cash
scenario.explain: Holders keep their rights while their shares are held safely; they can trade once they open accounts. Delaying for 100% coverage is unrealistic, and cancelling or selling without instruction is unlawful.

lessons.title: First-day price discovery
body: Shares that have never traded have no market price, and an introduction has no offer price. The first trades set the price. The ESX trades from 9:00 to 15:00 with a 30-minute pre-open session, in which orders are collected before trading starts, which helps form an opening price from accumulated buy and sell orders.

Advisers prepare for day one by publishing a reference value (for a combined introduction and offer, the offer price), encouraging institutions and brokers to place orders in the pre-open, and briefing holders not to sell in panic. The ESX lot size is one share, so even small holders can trade.
The ESX Rulebook does not set a settlement cycle, tick size or price limits, so check the current trading notices before you tell investors how the first day will work.

regulation.text: Trading runs from 9:00 to 15:00 with a 30-minute pre-open session; the lot size is one share. The Rulebook sets no settlement cycle, tick size or price limits.

example.title: Bank A's first morning
example.text: In the pre-open on Bank A's first day, brokers entered buy orders for 96,000 shares and sell orders for 61,000, most of the sellers being long-standing holders. The opening trade came at ETB 1,860, 3.3% above the ETB 1,800 offer price. By the close, 142,000 shares had traded, worth about ETB 266 million.

scenario.title: A wide spread on day one
scenario.situation: A small insurer listing only by introduction has no offer price. In the pre-open, the best buy order is ETB 210 and the best sell order is ETB 390.
scenario.question: What is the most useful step the adviser could have taken before listing?
options: Ask the ESX to fix the price
Publish a reference value and encourage informed orders from institutions and brokers in the pre-open, so the order book has depth around fair value
Tell holders not to trade for a year
scenario.explain: Without an offer price, depth in the order book comes from informed participants who know the company's value. Fixing prices or buying the market is not the adviser's role.

lessons.title: After listing: continuing obligations and liquidity
body: Listing begins a relationship with investors. The company must publish results and material information on time, hold proper general meetings, manage insider dealing risk and keep its float above the minimum. Investor relations should continue the education work: explain results simply, publish a dividend calendar and answer shareholder questions.

Liquidity is the measure of success. Encourage research coverage by brokers, keep holders informed, and consider a market maker if the rules allow. Track daily volume, number of trades and the share of holders who have traded.
Every successful listing makes the next one easier. ECM advisers who look after their issuers after listing build the reputation that wins the next mandate.
points: Investor relations and a dividend calendar
lessons.tip: Agree an investor relations plan for the first year before listing day, not after.

takeaways: Investor education is part of the deal: fair, balanced and consistent with the prospectus
Every subscription channel needs KYC, a share account, accepted terms and payment into a segregated account
Reconcile channel reports to money received daily, and explain every difference before allocation
A listing by introduction raises no money but needs a clean register, dematerialization and ready holders
The ESX pre-open helps first-day price discovery; prepare depth around a reference value

quiz.q: What does a listing by introduction raise for the company?
options: New capital equal to 10% of shares
quiz.explain: An introduction admits existing shares; no shares are sold.

quiz.q: Channels report ETB 620 million but the offer accounts show ETB 612 million. What happens next?
options: Trace the ETB 8 million difference before allocation
quiz.explain: Every reported birr must be traced to money received before allocation.

quiz.q: What are the ESX trading hours under the Rulebook?
quiz.explain: The Rulebook sets 9:00 to 15:00 with a 30-minute pre-open.

quiz.q: What must happen to the share register before dematerialization?
options: It must be published in newspapers
It must be cleaned and reconciled exactly to share capital
quiz.explain: The depository records must start from a verified register.

quiz.q: Which marketing message is acceptable?
options: Shares can rise or fall; read the prospectus risk factors before you apply
No risk, it is a bank
quiz.explain: Communications must be balanced and consistent with the prospectus.

quiz.q: What is the ESX lot size?
quiz.explain: The Rulebook sets a lot size of one share.

modules.title: Follow-ons, rights issues and the capstone mandate
modules.summary: Run rights issues and follow-ons to meet capital needs, compute the theoretical ex-rights price, arrange underwriting, and present a full mandate plan for Bank A.
objectives: Explain rights issue mechanics and compute the theoretical ex-rights price and the value of a right
Size a capital raise from NBE capital requirements and the bank's growth plan
Assess underwriting and standby options and their cost
Present an integrated offer structure, timetable and investor education plan as lead adviser

lessons.title: Rights issue mechanics
body: A rights issue offers new shares to existing holders in proportion to what they own, for example 1 new share for every 6 held, at a subscription price below the market price. It respects the pre-emption rights that the Commercial Code gives existing shareholders and is the usual route for a share company that needs capital from its own holders.

Holders can take up their rights, sell them if the rights are tradable, or let them lapse. Shares not taken up go to an excess application pool, an underwriter, or new investors, as the offer terms say. A deep discount makes take-up likely; it does not by itself transfer value, because every holder can subscribe.
The timetable runs from the general meeting resolution and the record date, through the subscription period, to allocation of excess shares and listing of the new shares.

items.label: Resolution
items.text: General meeting approves the capital increase

items.label: Record date
items.text: Holders on the register get rights

items.label: Subscription
items.text: Take up, sell or let rights lapse

items.label: Excess and shortfall
items.text: Excess applications, underwriter, new investors

items.label: New shares
items.text: Allotted and listed

example.title: A rights issue for capital
example.text: Bank A had used a rights issue in 2025 to lift its paid-up capital toward the ETB 5 billion minimum of SBB/78/2021. Holders took up 81% of their rights; the remaining shares went to existing holders who applied for excess. The board noted the lesson: a rights issue reaches only the existing base, which is why the 2026 raise also includes public tranches.

scenario.title: A holder who cannot pay
scenario.situation: A retired holder with 600 Bank A shares cannot afford the 100 new shares she is entitled to in a 1-for-6 rights issue. The rights are tradable on the ESX.
scenario.question: What should her broker explain?
options: She loses nothing if she does nothing
Her existing shares will be cancelled
She can sell her rights to capture their value instead of letting them lapse
scenario.explain: When the ex-rights price falls below the cum-rights price, a holder who neither subscribes nor sells loses value. Selling tradable rights compensates her.

lessons.title: The theoretical ex-rights price
body: After a rights issue at a discount, the share price should fall to a blend of the old price and the subscription price. This is the theoretical ex-rights price (TERP): the total value of the old shares plus the cash raised, divided by the total number of shares.

The value of a right is the difference between the TERP and the subscription price for each new share, or the difference between the cum-rights price and the TERP for each old share. A holder who takes up or sells her rights is no worse off; a holder who lets them lapse loses that value.
TERP is theoretical because it ignores what the market thinks of the use of the money. If investors believe the capital will earn more than its cost, the price may settle above TERP.

worked.title: Bank A: a 1-for-6 rights issue alternative

rows.label: Market price before the issue (cum rights)
Value of a right per new share (1,757.14 - 1,500)

worked.note: A 1-for-6 rights issue at ETB 1,500 raises about ETB 1.3 billion, short of the ETB 1.5 billion target, and reaches only existing holders. This supports the board's choice of a public offer.

scenario.title: Lapsing rights
scenario.situation: A holder with 6,000 shares lets all her rights lapse in the 1-for-6 issue above, and the rights are not sold for her.
scenario.question: Roughly what value does she lose, in theory?
scenario.explain: Each old share falls by about ETB 42.86 from 1,800 to the TERP of 1,757.14; 6,000 x 42.86 is about ETB 257,000.

lessons.title: Sizing a raise from capital requirements
body: For a bank, the size of the raise starts with the capital plan. Project risk-weighted assets from the growth plan, apply the SBB/95/2025 minimums (CET1 7%, Tier 1 9%, total capital 11%) plus the board's own buffer, and compare with projected capital including retained profits.

The paid-up capital minimum of ETB 5 billion under SBB/78/2021 (reported in the program register) was due for existing banks by 30 June 2026. Banks that met it through rights issues and retained earnings now face the risk-based ratios as the binding constraint.
Show the board the raise needed in three cases: the growth plan, a slower plan, and a stress case with higher provisions. The ECM raise should cover the growth plan with a buffer.

worked.title: Bank A: capital need for 2027

rows.label: Board target total capital ratio (11% minimum + 1.5% buffer)

worked.note: The ETB 1.5 billion offer is sized to hold a 12.5% total capital ratio through the growth plan, with a 1.5-point buffer over the SBB/95/2025 minimum.

regulation.source: NBE Directives No. SBB/95/2025 (capital adequacy) and SBB/78/2021 (minimum paid-up capital, reported)
regulation.text: Risk-based minimums of CET1 7%, Tier 1 9% and total capital 11% of risk-weighted assets, with full compliance by 31 December 2026. SBB/78/2021 is reported to set a minimum paid-up capital of ETB 5 billion for existing banks by 30 June 2026.

lessons.title: Underwriting and standby commitments
body: An underwriter agrees to buy any shares that investors do not take up, for a fee. In a firm underwriting the underwriter commits to the whole offer; in a standby arrangement, common for rights issues, it buys only the shortfall. Underwriting turns an uncertain raise into a certain one, which matters when a bank must meet a capital deadline.

In Ethiopia, underwriting capacity is still small. Investment banks licensed under ECMA Directive No. 980/2024 have limited balance sheets, so syndicates, sub-underwriting by insurers and pension funds, or a standby commitment from a strategic investor may be needed. Any standby investor in a bank who could end up with 2% or more needs NBE approval in advance.
The underwriting agreement sets the commitment, fee, conditions and termination rights. Advisers must check that the underwriter has the capital to honor it.

worked.title: Bank A: standby underwriting (illustrative terms)

rows.label: Expected take-up (soft sounding and retail survey)
Shortfall if take-up is ETB 1,300 million
Shares bought by standby investors at ETB 1,800
Largest standby investor's share of commitment

worked.note: The standby covers a shortfall well beyond the expected one, and no standby investor would reach the 2% NBE approval threshold even if called on in full.

scenario.title: An under-capitalized underwriter
scenario.situation: A small licensed investment bank offers to underwrite Bank A's full ETB 1.5 billion offer. Its own capital is ETB 150 million.
scenario.question: What should Bank A's adviser conclude?
options: Accept, a commitment is a commitment
The commitment is not credible without sub-underwriters or a syndicate; require evidence of capacity
Ask ESX to guarantee the underwriter
scenario.explain: An underwriter that could not pay if called on gives false certainty. Capacity must be backed by capital or committed sub-underwriters.

lessons.title: Follow-on offers by listed companies
body: Once listed, a company can raise more equity through a follow-on public offer, an accelerated placement with institutions, or a rights issue. The market price is now known, so pricing is set at a discount to the recent trading price rather than to an estimated fair value.

Follow-ons depend on the issuer's track record since listing: timely disclosure, a share price that has held up, and liquidity. They still need ECMA registration of the offer, shareholder approval of the capital increase and, for a bank, NBE engagement on large allocations.
Advisers should warn issuers that a follow-on soon after an IPO, at a lower price, damages trust. Plan the capital path for three years at the time of the IPO.

example.title: Selam's follow-on
example.text: Eighteen months after its Growth Board listing, Selam Agro Processing needed ETB 60 million for a second plant. Its shares had traded between ETB 95 and ETB 120, last at ETB 110. Liya Tadesse priced a follow-on at ETB 100, a 9.1% discount to the last price, and the shares were taken up by existing institutions and new retail investors within the offer period.

scenario.title: Placement or rights
scenario.situation: Two years after listing, Bank A needs ETB 800 million quickly. Its shares trade at ETB 2,050, and three pension funds want to buy new shares at ETB 1,950. Retail holders hold 60% of the shares.
scenario.question: What is the most balanced approach?
options: Place everything with the three funds at ETB 1,950, ignoring pre-emption
Combine a placement with the funds within the limits holders approve with a rights or open offer so retail holders can take part at the same price
scenario.explain: Speed from a placement plus fairness through a rights or open offer protects the retail majority and respects pre-emption, which holders must waive for a pure placement.

lessons.title: Capstone: the Bank A mandate plan
body: In the capstone, teams act as lead adviser to Bank A for its listing by introduction plus an ETB 1.5 billion capital raise. The deliverable is a mandate pitch and offer plan covering: the readiness assessment and fixes, the offer structure (primary shares, tranches, clawback, allocation), the valuation and pricing method, the ECMA and ESX filings and fees, the NBE approvals, the subscription channels and reconciliation, the register clean-up and dematerialization, the investor education plan, and the full timetable.

Assessment follows the specification: the mandate pitch and offer plan carry 40%, a test 30%, a work assignment (a readiness assessment of a real company) 20% and participation 10%. The pass mark is 70%.

Judges look for internal consistency: the raise matches the capital need, the float and moratorium are respected, every allocation over 2% is conditional on NBE approval, and the timetable allows for audit, ECMA comments and account opening.

items.label: Month 1
items.text: Mandate, readiness review, register audit starts

items.label: Months 2 to 3
items.text: Due diligence, audited accounts signed, general meeting resolution

items.label: Month 4
items.text: Prospectus filed with ECMA, ESX listing application, NBE pre-clearance

items.label: Month 5
items.text: ECMA comments answered, investor education campaign, institutional sounding

items.label: Month 6
items.text: Price fixed, offer period, daily reconciliation

items.label: Month 7
items.text: Allocation, refunds, dematerialization, listing day

worked.title: Capstone summary: Bank A offer plan

rows.label: Listing
rows.value: ESX Main Board by introduction, 5,200,000 existing shares

rows.label: New money
rows.value: ETB 1.5 billion, 833,333 primary shares at ETB 1,800

rows.label: Pricing
rows.value: Hybrid: institutional sounding, fixed retail price

rows.label: Valuation
rows.value: P/B 1.17x after the offer, P/E 8.0x, 14.3% IPO discount

rows.label: Capital ratio after the raise (growth plan)

worked.note: A plan whose numbers tie together across capital need, size, price, float and fees is what wins the mandate.

scenario.title: A judge's challenge
scenario.situation: In the capstone pitch, a judge notes that a team's plan allocates 6% of the enlarged shares to one pension fund in the institutional tranche and shows listing in month 5.
scenario.question: Which two weaknesses should the team fix?
options: The 6% allocation needs NBE approval as a 2%-plus holding and must be conditional, and month 5 leaves too little time for audit, ECMA comments and account opening
None, the plan is aggressive but fine
Listing should be moved to month 2
scenario.explain: A bank allocation above 2% requires NBE approval, and a realistic timetable must include the audit, ECMA review and dematerialization steps.

takeaways: A rights issue respects pre-emption; holders take up, sell or let rights lapse
TERP = (old shares x price + new shares x subscription price) / total shares
Size a bank's raise from projected RWA, the SBB/95/2025 minimums and a board buffer
Underwriting commitments are only as good as the underwriter's capacity, and bank standby investors must stay below 2% or get NBE approval
A winning mandate plan ties capital need, structure, price, float, fees, approvals and timetable together

quiz.q: A share trades at ETB 600. A 1-for-4 rights issue is priced at ETB 450. What is the TERP?
In the example above, what is the value of a right per new share?
quiz.explain: TERP 570 minus subscription price 450 = ETB 120.

quiz.q: What does a standby underwriter commit to?
options: Buying the whole offer at a fixed price
Buying only the shares not taken up
quiz.explain: A standby commitment covers only the shortfall.

quiz.q: A bank's RWA will be ETB 50 billion and the board targets 12% total capital. Projected capital is ETB 5.4 billion. How much must it raise?
quiz.explain: 50 x 12% = 6.0 billion; 6.0 minus 5.4 = ETB 0.6 billion.

quiz.q: Why is a follow-on at a lower price soon after an IPO harmful?
options: It breaks the ESX lot size
It erodes IPO investors' trust and suggests poor capital planning
quiz.explain: Investors who bought at the IPO lose value and trust; plan the capital path at the IPO.

quiz.q: Which capstone component carries the largest weight?
quiz.explain: The mandate pitch and offer plan count for 40%.

exam.q: Gondar Cement has ETB 1.8 billion market capitalization and plans a Main Board listing. Insiders hold 87% and 900 others hold 13%. What must change?
options: The public float must rise to at least 15%, since market capitalization is below ETB 2 billion
It must move to the Fixed Income Market
exam.explain: Below ETB 2 billion the float test is 15% held by at least 300 holders.

exam.q: A company lost money in all of the last 3 years but grew revenue 30% a year for 3 years and has a market capitalization of ETB 120 million. Where can it list?
options: Growth Board, if it places at least 10% with at least 50 holders
Main Board after one profitable quarter
exam.explain: The Growth Board has no profit test; the Main Board needs profit at least once in 3 years and ETB 500 million size.

exam.q: What is the ECMA registration fee for an ETB 2.4 billion share offer?
exam.explain: ETB 300,000 plus 0.1% of ETB 2.4 billion (ETB 2.4 million) is ETB 2.7 million.

exam.q: An investor sells ETB 5 million of listed shares. What is the ECMA transaction fee?
exam.explain: 0.15% of ETB 5 million is ETB 7,500.

exam.q: A founder with 3 million shares lists on the Growth Board. Within 12 months he may sell at most:
exam.explain: Insiders may sell at most 50% of their holding in the first 12 months.

exam.q: Which is the strongest lesson for deal design from the Ethio telecom 2024 offer?
options: Retail investors cannot be reached digitally
Wide digital reach needs to be paired with sound price discovery, a liquidity path and investor education
Fixed prices always guarantee full take-up
exam.explain: Reach was proven; reported take-up shows the importance of pricing, liquidity and familiarity.

exam.q: Bank A's prospectus says proceeds will fund 'digital expansion' with no breakdown. What is the main problem?
options: Use of proceeds must be specific and tied to the business plan
exam.explain: Investors and ECMA expect amounts, purposes and timing linked to the plan.

exam.q: Which readiness issue most often delays filing?
options: Missing audited IFRS accounts for the track record period
exam.explain: Without audited accounts the prospectus cannot be completed or filed.

exam.q: A company has 10 million shares and raises ETB 900 million at ETB 300 per share. What is the post-offer stake of new investors?
exam.explain: 900 million / 300 = 3 million new shares; 3 / 13 million = 23.1%.

exam.q: Fair value is ETB 1,200 per share and the offer price is ETB 1,020 with 500,000 new shares. How much value goes to new investors through the discount?
Institutional bids are ETB 400 million at ETB 950 and ETB 620 million at ETB 900; the institutional tranche is ETB 500 million. Which price gives cover with a cushion?
exam.explain: At ETB 900, 620 / 500 = 1.24x; at ETB 950 the tranche is uncovered.

exam.q: Why would a bank issuer's P/B of 1.1x not necessarily be cheap?
options: Because a high birr cost of equity and a modest ROE can justify a multiple near 1x
exam.explain: Fair P/B rises with ROE relative to the cost of equity; in birr the cost of equity is high.

exam.q: A draft plan includes a 15% over-allotment and stabilization. What is the right treatment?
options: Keep it, it is global practice
Keep it but do not disclose it
Leave it out unless ECMA confirms a legal basis and the disclosure required
exam.explain: Stabilization needs explicit legal permission; Ethiopian rules on it are not confirmed in the available texts.

exam.q: A retail tranche of ETB 300 million receives ETB 900 million of applications. Small applicants take ETB 120 million in full. At what rate are larger applicants filled if they applied for ETB 780 million?
exam.explain: Remaining ETB 180 million / ETB 780 million = 23.1%.

exam.q: Channels report ETB 410 million of subscriptions, accounts show ETB 404 million, and ETB 6 million of checks are uncleared. How should the checks be treated?
options: Exclude them from allocation until they clear, or reject the applications
Ask the issuer to cover them
exam.explain: Only cleared money supports an allocation.

exam.q: In a listing by introduction with no offer price, what most helps a sensible opening price?
options: A fixed price set by the ESX
A rights issue on day one
A published reference value and informed orders in the 30-minute pre-open
exam.explain: Depth from informed participants in the pre-open supports price discovery; the Rulebook sets no price limits.

exam.q: A share trades at ETB 900. A 1-for-5 rights issue is priced at ETB 600. What is the TERP?
A bank projects RWA of ETB 120 billion and targets 12.5% total capital. Capital before the raise will be ETB 13.8 billion. What raise is needed?
exam.explain: 120 x 12.5% = 15.0 billion; 15.0 minus 13.8 = ETB 1.2 billion.

exam.q: A standby investor in a bank rights issue could end up with 3.5% of the shares if called on fully. What is required?
options: Prior NBE approval under SBB/89/2024, or a smaller commitment that stays below 2%
exam.explain: Holdings of 2% or more in a bank need NBE approval, so the commitment must be approved or capped.

exam.q: A listed company needs capital fast and three institutions offer to buy at a 5% discount, while retail holds 55%. What is the fairest structure?
options: A placement to the institutions only, without shareholder approval
A placement within limits holders approve, combined with a rights or open offer to retail at the same price
exam.explain: Combining speed with an offer to retail holders respects pre-emption and fairness.
